body:
Discipline draft for ratification — the brief-implementability rule, plus STORY-1391 for the detection half

The operator asked where tonight's rework lesson should live: encoded, or gated by an agent. The answer is both and they do different jobs, so I have split it.

STORY-1391 carries the DETECTION, filed Draft. Its first step is a blocker neither of us had noticed: `.aida/review-verdicts/PR-N.json` is OVERWRITTEN each round. 510 files, one per PR plus an `-advisor` variant, no round history. So round N's findings are destroyed when round N+1 is recorded and nothing can compare them. TASK-168 merged tonight adding reviewed_sha and recorded_at, so per-verdict provenance now exists — what is missing is not discarding the previous one.

Three design constraints I wrote in deliberately, because this is easy to build wrong:
- the signal must point at the BRIEF, not the implementer. "This finding survived a round, check it is implementable as written" produces a different action from "the implementer failed again", and the second framing produces exactly the escalating firmness that failed three times tonight.
- no blocking, no round-count threshold. TASK-1289 went five rounds and needed a design decision, not an automatic park.
- matching must tolerate rewording, with the spec stating what test it uses and what it misses. An exact-match would have caught none of tonight's three. I gave it a negative fixture too — BUG-1297's round 3 carried a genuinely NEW finding alongside the persistent one, and flagging that would teach people to ignore the signal.

THE DRAFT BELOW is the reasoning half, for session-discipline.md. Not merged — the pack ships downstream and it is yours to ratify, same as the reviewer-independence entry.

One thing I want to flag about my own framing in it. I wrote the rule as "the requirement has no available mechanism", which is what the three cases showed. But I have only three cases and they are all mine, so the generalisation may be too confident. If you think "the implementer could not see what to do" is doing work that "the implementer did not do it" would sometimes do better, narrow it — I would rather the entry be true than tidy.

The worked examples are deliberately stated without spec ids, since the pack ships to projects where ours mean nothing.

--- DRAFT BEGINS ---
## A finding that survives a round is evidence about the brief

When a reviewer raises the same finding twice, the natural reading is that the
implementer did not do it. That reading leads to restating the requirement more
firmly — numbering it, adding acceptance criteria, marking it binding. Sometimes
that works. When it does not, the second reading is usually the true one:

**the requirement has no available mechanism, and saying it louder cannot supply
one.**

An implementer who can see what to do generally does it. An implementer who
cannot see what to do, given an instruction phrased as an outcome, has no way to
say so — there is no "this is not implementable as written" move in a rework
round. So the finding comes back unchanged, which looks exactly like not trying.

### What this looks like

Three specs, one night, all of them stuck for the same reason and all of them
moving as soon as the brief carried a mechanism instead of an outcome.

**"Use one shared constant for the marker."** The writer was a markdown template;
the reader was Rust. A markdown file cannot import a Rust constant, so the
requirement was not implementable in its own terms. It went three rounds — advice,
then numbered requirement — and moved the round the brief contained a ten-line
coupling test that reads the template and asserts it contains the constant.

**"Enumerate every external-tool prose classifier."** No terminating condition:
nothing in the instruction said what counted as one, so no answer could be known
to be complete. Two rounds. It moved when the brief carried the enumerated sites
and a three-part definition of what belongs in the inventory.

**"Type the outcome rather than matching the error text."** Correct, and still
abstract. Two rounds. It moved when the brief carried the enum and the rewritten
match arms.

### How to apply

- **When a finding survives a round, stop restating it.** Escalating firmness is
  the wrong response to an impossible request; it only makes the same request
  louder. Go and establish whether it can be done as written.
- **Supply a mechanism, not an outcome.** The code, the enumerated list, the
  terminating definition, the file and line. Ten lines of example beat a
  paragraph of requirement.
- **If you cannot supply one, say that.** "This is blocked on X" or "split this"
  are both better than a third restatement. A brief that admits a gap is
  actionable; one that hides it is not.
- **Offer partial credit explicitly.** "If only one of these fits this round, do
  the first and state that the second is outstanding." A round closing one of two
  findings is progress; a round closing neither is not, and an implementer given
  no priority will often attempt the harder one and run out of budget before the
  easy one.
- **Watch for the shape where the two sides live in different languages or
  systems** — a template and its reader, a config and its consumer, a doc and the
  code it describes. Coupling those is where "just share a constant" stops being
  available, and it is the most common source of this failure.

### Why a rule and not a habit

Noticing a repeat requires holding the previous round's findings while reading the
current ones. Rework briefs are usually written from the current verdict alone, by
whoever is awake. This is worth a mechanical signal rather than vigilance — and
if your substrate overwrites a verdict each round, the history a signal would need
is being destroyed, which is its own thing to fix first.
--- DRAFT ENDS ---
